justifications.functional_suitability: The architecture satisfies R-01, R-02, and R-03 thoroughly. The Claims Web Application serves Customers, Brokers, and Claims Adjusters, while the Integration & Anti-Corruption Layer and Routing Registry Component explicitly manage the incremental migration of claim types.
justifications.performance_efficiency: R-05 is directly met by decoupling adjuster reads from the 5-second mainframe response via Read Model Projections in the New Claims Database, asynchronous message handling via Azure Service Bus, and client-side caching in the Claim Form & Validation Component.
justifications.compatibility: The Mainframe Adapter and Claim Translation Component form an effective Anti-Corruption Layer connecting to the COBOL/DB2 mainframe over ExpressRoute/mTLS. Coexistence is well-architected, and SSO integration with on-premise Active Directory is supported via standard OIDC/SAML protocols.
justifications.usability: All target personas (Customers, Brokers, Adjusters) are provided dedicated interaction paths through the Claims Dashboard and Claim Form components with RBAC routing. However, hosting both public submission and internal adjuster workflows in a single web application container introduces minor usability compromises.
justifications.reliability: R-04 is achieved through the Outbox Schema, Sync & Reconciliation Router with dead-letter queues, and Sync Tracking Schema. Fault tolerance is reinforced by Polly circuit breakers in the Mainframe Adapter and Routing Dispatcher.
justifications.security: R-07 is satisfied via Active Directory integration for SSO. Confidentiality and integrity are enforced using Azure Key Vault with Managed Identities, mTLS between internal components, TDE, and Private Link isolation.
justifications.maintainability: R-06 is handled via the Routing Registry Component in Azure App Configuration for fast rollbacks. The Anti-Corruption Layer provides clean decoupling, though the high number of distributed Azure PaaS services adds operational complexity for a team with little cloud experience.
justifications.portability: The design satisfies the hybrid deployment topology between on-premise and Azure West Europe. However, tight coupling to proprietary Azure PaaS services (Azure Static Web Apps, App Configuration, Service Bus, Key Vault) significantly limits infrastructure replaceability.

PERF-01.justification: Read Model Projections in Azure SQL and client-side caching serve UI requests under 2 seconds, shielding adjusters from 5-second mainframe calls. However, explicit pre-fetching or asynchronous mirroring for legacy claim slices is not fully detailed.
sensitivity_points: Eventual consistency lag between mainframe updates and read model projections
tradeoffs: Data freshness sacrificed for low screen latency

PERF-02.justification: Scale spikes are absorbed by Azure Container Apps and queued asynchronously via Azure Service Bus and the Outbox pattern. Batching and rate-limited throttling towards the mainframe adapter prevent any impact on the nightly batch window.
sensitivity_points: Service Bus queue capacity and consumer rate limits during month-end spikes
tradeoffs: Immediate customer submission acceptance traded against delayed mainframe persistence

AVAIL-01.justification: The transactional outbox and Azure Service Bus buffer submissions durably while the mainframe is offline during the batch window. Once available, messages are processed without loss.
sensitivity_points: Storage retention and DLQ thresholds during extended mainframe downtime
tradeoffs: Storage overhead in outbox tables to guarantee delivery during downtime

AVAIL-02.justification: Sync Tracking Schema with SQL bulk reconciliation, Azure Service Bus DLQs, and Polly retry policies in the Mainframe Adapter handle partial sync failures and enforce idempotency to prevent duplicate processing.
sensitivity_points: Idempotency key consistency across modern and legacy mainframe schemas
tradeoffs: Reconciliation logic complexity versus strict at-least-once message processing

MOD-01.justification: The Anti-Corruption Layer isolates legacy interfaces, while the Routing Registry using Azure App Configuration provides dynamic feature flags that allow rerouting or rolling back claim types within minutes without code redeployments.
sensitivity_points: Granularity of feature flag toggles per claim type in App Configuration
tradeoffs: Operational overhead of maintaining dual routing logic and schemas

MOD-02.justification: Frontend applications depend strictly on the API Gateway & BFF. When the mainframe is retired, only the Integration & Anti-Corruption Layer is decommissioned; UI layers require zero rewrites.
sensitivity_points: Decoupling quality between BFF endpoints and legacy-specific data contracts
tradeoffs: BFF abstraction layer maintenance cost during the multi-year migration period

SEC-01.justification: YARP API Router and Auth & RBAC components enforce authentication and basic permissions, logged via Application Insights. However, fine-grained object-level authorization (broker-to-customer ownership validation) is not explicitly formalized.
sensitivity_points: Enforcement point of domain-level multi-tenancy and data ownership checks
tradeoffs: BFF-layer authorization logic complexity versus generic gateway pass-through

SEC-02.justification: SSO integrates both environments with Active Directory. Terminating an adjuster in AD halts access, but short-lived token lifetimes or active session invalidation across both Azure Static Web Apps and legacy systems are not detailed.
sensitivity_points: OAuth2 access token expiration times and token revocation handling
tradeoffs: Frequent token re-validation overhead versus rapid access revocation
